column1: # Short flags declared `standalone` in one scope of a command while another scope of the SAME
# WHY THIS EXISTS. The short-flag half of `flag_arity_worklist.tsv`. A valued flag mismodelled as
# `standalone` lets its value fall through as a POSITIONAL, so any gate on the flag never fires.
# Comparing a short flag across tools carries no information (`-o` is an output path in one tool
# and a boolean in the next), but within ONE tool a letter usually keeps its meaning from
# subcommand to subcommand, so the tool's own entry is the comparison.
# HOW THE CANDIDATES ARE PICKED. A short flag standalone-only in one scope (the command, a nested
# sub, the fallback, a `handler_policy` block, the `behavior` grammar) and valued-only in another
# scope of the same command. A flag in both lists of a scope, or in `optional_valued`, is neither.
# IT IS A HEURISTIC, NOT A VERDICT. Suites of separate programs (git, cargo, docker) reuse letters
# freely, so many rows are correct as written: `git status -s` is a boolean and `git merge -s`
# names a strategy. Resolving a row means checking that one scope's grammar, then moving the flag
# to `valued` / `optional_valued`, or adding a `# right: <reason>` comment line above the row.
# A correct row stays listed: the guard cannot tell it apart, and removing it fails the test.
# a candidate that is not listed and on a listed row that is no longer a candidate.
